title: Tarski fixed-point search belongs to CLS and EOPL
formal: Does the total search problem \(\mathrm{Tarski}\) defined below belong to \(\mathrm{CLS}\), and also to \(\mathrm{EOPL}\), under deterministic polynomial-time search reductions? Both answers are affirmative: the source proves \(\mathrm{Tarski}\in\mathrm{PLS}\cap\mathrm{PPAD}\), and the subsequent equalities \(\mathrm{CLS}=\mathrm{PLS}\cap\mathrm{PPAD}=\mathrm{EOPL}\) settle both membership alternatives in its question.
why: The classification connects a basic order-theoretic existence theorem with continuous local search and directed paths carrying an increasing potential. It also illustrates how a theorem equating complexity classes can resolve earlier membership questions without directly solving their search problems in polynomial time.
status_note: Resolved affirmatively for both classes. The source proves the same totalized circuit problem lies in PLS ∩ PPAD; the full-version proofs of Theorems 3.2–3.3 and Corollary 3.4 were read. Fearnley–Goldberg–Hollender–Savani (STOC 2021, Theorems 6.1/6.4) give CLS = PLS ∩ PPAD, and Göös et al. (CCC 2022, Theorem 1) give EOPL = PLS ∩ PPAD and explicitly state the Tarski consequence. The latter’s definition equivalence and main reductions were checked. Thus neither source membership alternative remains open. This review is not a claim of a new independent proof or an existing Lean formalization.

progress.text: The source proves Tarski ∈ PLS ∩ PPAD and asks about the finer CLS and EOPL memberships.

category_assignment.reason: The target asks whether Tarski fixed-point search lies in CLS or EOPL, a total-search complexity classification.

importance.reason: A natural fixed-point search classification linking order theory, equilibria and total-search complexity. Both source membership questions are resolved by the 2021 and 2022 class equalities.

sentences: Tarski search receives a Boolean circuit on a finite multidimensional grid.
It must return any fixed point or a pair witnessing a violation of monotonicity.
The original source proved membership in both PLS and PPAD and asked whether finer CLS or EOPL membership also held.
Published class equalities from 2021 and 2022 establish both memberships for precisely this totalized problem.
The record is therefore resolved and archived, without asserting polynomial-time solvability or membership in UEOPL.

definitions:
An instance of Tarski consists of positive integers \(d,b\) and an explicit Boolean circuit \(C\) with \(db\) input bits and \(db\) output bits, using AND, OR and NOT gates. Interpret each consecutive block of \(b\) bits as an integer in \(\{0,\ldots,2^b-1\}\). The circuit therefore defines a total function \(f:D\to D\), with
\[D=\{0,\ldots,2^b-1\}^{d}.\]
The coordinate-wise order is \(x\le y\) if \(x_i\le y_i\) for every \(i\in[d]\). A fixed point has \(f(x)=x\). Monotonicity means \(x\le y\Rightarrow f(x)\le f(y)\) for every pair in \(D\).

A valid output is either a tagged fixed point \(x\in D\), or a tagged pair \(x,y\in D\) with \(x\le y\) and \(f(x)\not\le f(y)\); the latter means \(f(x)_i>f(y)_i\) for at least one coordinate. No promise of monotonicity is required. If the circuit is monotone, a fixed point exists by Tarski's theorem. If it is not, a violation pair exists, and either a fixed point or a violation is acceptable when both exist. Any fixed point suffices; the least, greatest or unique fixed point is not requested. Both \(d\) and \(b\) may grow with the input. Circuit gates, connections, all input/output wires and the integers specifying their widths are explicit, so \(db\) is bounded by the input length. Coordinates and witnesses use binary encoding. Shifting coordinates by one gives the source's convention \([2^b]^d\).

A deterministic polynomial-time search reduction from problem \(A\) to problem \(B\) consists of two ordinary Turing algorithms \(F,H\). For every valid instance \(I\), \(F(I)\) is a valid instance of \(B\), and for every permitted solution \(z\) of \(F(I)\), \(H(I,z)\) is a permitted solution of \(I\). Both run in polynomially many bit operations in the lengths of their explicit inputs. Thus the reduction must handle every target solution, not only a preferred one. Syntactically malformed inputs can be given a distinguished invalid-input output, checkable in polynomial time.

The following published equivalent complete problems fix the two target classes without relying on an informal meaning of continuous or potential.

For CLS, use two-dimensional linear Continuous-Localopt. An instance gives a positive binary rational \(\varepsilon\) and finite linear arithmetic circuits for \(p:[0,1]^2\to[0,1]\) and \(g:[0,1]^2\to[0,1]^2\). Gates are addition, subtraction, minimum, maximum, multiplication by a binary rational constant, and rational constants; there is no multiplication of two computed quantities. Clamp output coordinates to \([0,1]\) with minimum and maximum, so their range is guaranteed syntactically. Return a binary rational point \(x\in[0,1]^2\) satisfying
\[p(g(x))\ge p(x)-\varepsilon.\]
This is the approximate local-optimum condition for the improvement map \(g\); it does not ask for a global minimum. The circuits are continuous and have effective finite Lipschitz bounds, and valid solutions of polynomial bit length exist. CLS is the class of total polynomially verifiable search relations reducible to this problem. The equivalence to the original CLS definition is Theorem 6.4 of the cited STOC paper. The tolerance \(\varepsilon\) is part of this auxiliary search input, not an approximation allowance on the card's membership assertion.

For EOPL, use the equivalent layered End-of-Potential-Line formulation from the CCC paper. Its instance contains positive binary integers \(N\ge1,M\ge2\) and explicit Boolean circuits \(S,P\) that, on a grid point \((i,j)\in[N]\times[M]\), return an index in \([N]\) or a null symbol. There is a directed edge from \((i,j)\) to \((i',j+1)\) exactly when \(j<M\), \(S(i,j)=i'\in[N]\), and \(P(i',j+1)=i\). Out-of-range circuit values are treated as null. Thus the two pointers are checked for consistency by definition, every vertex has indegree and outdegree at most one, and the potential given by the column number strictly increases on every edge.

The distinguished start is \((1,1)\). A solution is that point if it has no outgoing edge, or any other source or any sink in the resulting graph. A source has outdegree one and indegree zero; a sink has indegree one and outdegree zero. Other isolated vertices are not solutions. The path from the distinguished start guarantees a solution. The graph may have many other paths, and its grid is represented by the circuits and binary bounds rather than by an explicit list of all vertices. Solutions have binary coordinates. EOPL is the class of total polynomially verifiable search relations reducible to this problem. This formulation is polynomially equivalent to the usual one with an explicit potential circuit; it does not impose the unique-path restriction of UEOPL.
answer_criterion: A complete Lean-checked proof of each membership must provide polynomial-time instance and solution transformations to the corresponding complete problem, or formally compose established reductions and class-equality theorems that provide them. The proof must cover unbounded input dimension and the totalized Tarski relation, including every allowed non-monotonicity witness. These are exact search-class memberships; a polynomial-time algorithm only at fixed dimension, a query bound without a polynomial bit-time reduction, or an algorithm for an extremal fixed point is a different claim. The published mathematical resolution recorded here does not assert that these proofs have already been formalized in Lean.

source_formulation.text: The source asks whether its Tarski total search problem belongs to CLS, or to the then potentially smaller class EOPL.
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of the membership question in §6; both alternatives were subsequently resolved affirmatively

context_blocks.text: Tarski’s theorem guarantees a fixed point for an order-preserving map on a finite lattice. The computational problem gives the map as a small circuit, so the lattice may be exponentially larger than the input. Finding any fixed point can therefore be difficult even though verifying one is easy.

The source removes a promise that would be hard to check: if the map is not monotone, a pair witnessing failure is also a valid output. This makes the task a total search problem on all syntactically valid circuits and lets its complexity be compared with other total-search classes.

The original paper proves membership in both PLS and PPAD. Informally these classes express the existence of a local optimum and of an endpoint forced by directed parity. At publication, belonging to both classes did not yet imply membership in the more structured class CLS.

The 2021 gradient-descent theorem identifies CLS with the intersection PLS ∩ PPAD. Consequently the original Tarski membership theorem already gives an affirmative answer to the CLS part. The result supplies a classification by reductions; it does not give a polynomial-time algorithm for all instances.

The 2022 collapse theorem identifies EOPL with the same intersection and explicitly notes Tarski among its consequences. Hence the apparently stronger EOPL alternative is also settled. UEOPL requires an additional uniqueness structure and is a different class, so a question about UEOPL would not be the original membership question.
